title: Momentum
subject: Physics

English.simple_explanation: Momentum tells us how much motion an object has. A heavier object or a faster object has more momentum.
English.detailed_explanation: Linear momentum is mass multiplied by velocity: p = m x v. Because velocity includes direction, momentum also has direction.
English.everyday_example: A moving loaded cart is usually harder to stop than a moving empty cart at the same speed.

local_example.text: Comparing a loaded transport vehicle with a bicycle is a useful way to reason about why a larger moving mass can be harder to stop.
local_example.appropriate_usage: Present as an engineering illustration; do not treat it as a claim about a specific local route or occupation.

common_misconceptions: A fast light object can have more momentum than a slow heavy object.
think_question: Why is it usually harder to stop a moving truck than a moving bicycle?

reasoning_guide.correct_feedback: Good reasoning: you connected the larger mass to greater momentum.
reasoning_guide.partial_feedback: You are close. Explain how mass changes momentum, not only how fast something moves.
reasoning_guide.misconception_feedback: Speed matters, but mass matters too. Compare both when reasoning about momentum.

challenge.question: A 2 kg object moves at 5 m/s. What is its momentum?
progressive_hints: Substitute 2 for mass and 5 for velocity before multiplying.
Write the unit as kg m/s after you calculate the number.
challenge.solution: Momentum = 2 kg x 5 m/s = 10 kg m/s.

quiz_questions.question: A 3 kg cart moves at 4 m/s. What is its momentum?
quiz_questions.explanation: Momentum = mass x velocity = 3 x 4 = 12 kg m/s.
quiz_questions.hint: Multiply the mass by the velocity.
progressive_hints: Multiply the mass by the velocity.
Calculate 3 x 4, then include kg m/s.
